transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
delivered his remarks yesterday to the UN General Assembly.
Many other world leaders this week have sharply criticized the Israeli government.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf says Netanyahu responded to the criticism.
He downplayed settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, saying it was the
work of 150 juvenile delinquents.
The UK recently said such settler attacks and land grabs amount to "ethnic cleansing."
Netanyahu rejected claims that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, something that's
come up repeatedly from other world leaders this week.
He also accused the media of not telling the "truth" about what's happening in Gaza.
But just a reminder, Israel has not allowed outside journalists to enter Gaza to independently
report in almost three years the entirety of this war.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf reporting.
Despite over press, freedom in the United States continues to play out against the backdrop
of President Trump's summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, now underway in Washington.
Journalists from CNN and MS Now were turned away from a White House state dinner last
night.
NPR's Brian Mann reports.
At least three journalists were denied access to the Trump dinner Thursday night, hours
after a federal judge on Thursday ordered the White House to reinstate press passes
for reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.
Meanwhile, the five major TV networks that normally provide pool video coverage of Trump
continued to boycott that operation in protest.
They want written reassurances that CNN will receive equal treatment and access without
government interference.
Other news outlets, including NPR, have also scaled back coverage.
Trump complained on social media about the lack of full coverage of the summit in front
of Xi.
Trump said how much he preferred the Chinese press to his own.
The Chinese communist government has been notoriously repressive toward independent journalists.
Brian Mann, NPR News.
A Republican-led Senate has narrowly blocked a resolution to end the war in Iran.
NPR's Claudia Grisales reports lawmakers split on the Democratic-led effort.
The resolution urging Trump to end hostilities against Iran failed by one vote.
Democrats forced this vote to happen.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune called the move political, but he conceded many GOP members
are ready for the war to be over.
I think there are a lot of Republican members.
Yes, obviously, everybody wants to see wars come to a conclusion.
Four Republicans joined Democrats to approve the measure, which was not legally binding.
However, one Democrat, John Federman of Pennsylvania, joined Republicans to vote the measure down.
Thune argued the administration is doing everything it can to end the conflict and take, quote,
the pressure of the American people's pocketbooks via lower prices at the pump for gasoline.
Claudia Grisales, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Forecasters say Hurricane NOLO is approaching Hawaii.
It's not expected to hit the islands, but nearly two feet of rain are expected to inundate
the Big Island.
Coffee retailer Starbucks says it plans to close 250 stores in North America this week.
This is the second wave of store closures under CEO Brian Nichol.
NPR's Alina Seljuk reports.
In a notice to employees, Starbucks did not say how many stores it's closing in the U.S.
versus Canada or how many of the stores are unionized.
The company says affected employees would be transferred or offered severance.
CEO Brian Nichol has been trying to cut $2 billion in annual costs by 2028.
Last year, he closed more than 600 stores and cut more than 1,000 corporate jobs.
All this is funding his turnaround plan, updating the menus, speeding up service and renovating
some locations, adding sofas and reusable mugs, trying to get people to spend more time
at the Starbucks cafes.
And the plan is showing results with customer visits and sales growing, but costs continue
to eat away at profits.
Alina Seljuk, NPR News.
Some states and cities are celebrating this as Dolly Parton Day.
Today is September 25th or 9 to 5.
Working 9 to 5, what a way to make a living, getting by, it's all taken and no given...
Many areas have issued proclamations to honor today that also shares the title of Dolly Parton's
song about working people 9 to 5.
Dolly Parton died about a month ago at the age of 80 after a short battle with cancer.
This is NPR.
